newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden divided over state's alcohol monopoly.
newsitem.headline: Sweden divided over state's alcohol monopoly.

text.p: Sweden was divided on Wednesday over whether the state should end its monopoly on alcohol sales and fall in line with a recommendation by a European Court.
Key Swedish politicians were adamant that the state's alcohol chain, the Systembolaget, should remain the only vendor of wine and spirits in the country.
"Under no circumstances could there be talk of fully liberalising the sale of alcohol, through grocery stores for example," Social Minister Margot Wallstrom said in a statement.
But the general public and shopkeepers wanted freer access to alcohol that is now only on sale during working hours, five days a week, in the state-owned stores.
"The Systembolaget's monopoly on the sale of wine and spirits in Sweden must be broken," said an editorial in tabloid paper Aftonbladet on Wednesday.

Sweden's state monopoly on the retail sale of alcohol came into question on Tuesday when an adviser at the European Court of Justice said European Union law was an "obstacle" to such retail sales regimes for alcohol.

Advocate-General Michael Elmer rejected the Swedish government's argument that the monopoly was justified on social and health grounds because of the country's traditionally high levels of alcohol consumption.
Although Elmer's opinion is only advisory, often the advocate-general's line is taken by the court in final rulings.
A district court in the Swedish town of Landskrona asked the EU court for a preliminary ruling on whether the monopoly was compatible with EU law.

The action was brought by the Landskrona public prosecutor against grocer Harry Franzen for breaking the Systembolaget monopoly over sales of wine and spirits, selling one-litre, sealed packs of white and red wines from his shop.
Franzen, who has become a popular figure in Sweden, was delighted by the preliminary ruling, celebrating with a glass of wine.
"If shops can sell wine it will help both them and the districts to survive," Franzen told Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter.
"I'm in favour of freedom and against all monopolies whether it's Systembolagets, chemists, or (betting shops) Tipstjanst."
The alcohol monopoly is an important source of revenue for the government. In 1996 sales at the Systembolagets reached about 19 billion crowns.
Nordic neighbours Norway and Iceland also operate state liquor monopolies.
Grocery store chains around Sweden were already prepared to start selling alcohol off their shelves.
A recent survey found 89 percent of owners of ICA grocery stores wanted to sell wine and full strength beer.

"It is a natural buying environment with food and drink together instead of people having to go to a special shop with the sole reason to buy alcohol products," Goran Doneleus, product leader for alcohol at ICA said.
The preliminary decision will be put to a full court for a final verdict in a few months time.
